title: Inject an overridable clock into streakMilestoneAnalyticsObserverProvider instead of hardcoding SystemLocalDayClock
why: The observer instantiates `const SystemLocalDayClock()` directly rather than watching an injectable clock — the codebase already has this seam elsewhere (e.g. outbox_providers.dart reads `ref.watch(localDayClockProvider)`). Because the observer can't be handed a fixed clock in tests, the happy-path test has to anchor seeded data to real `DateTime.now()` and then poll every 20ms for up to 5 real seconds waiting for the milestone to fire, instead of asserting deterministically against a fixed instant. The test's own comment documents this was already a source of past flakiness ('silently breaks the moment the calendar advances', 'failed in isolation') — the current polling approach is less likely to fail, not deterministic, and burns up to 5 real seconds per run.
recommendation: Thread a LocalDayClock through the provider (watch a clock provider, mirroring outbox_providers.dart) so tests can override with a fixed clock and assert the milestone fires on an exact expected tick without polling.
acceptance_criteria: streak_milestone_analytics_observer_test.dart's happy-path test uses a fixed/injected clock instead of DateTime.now(), with no wall-clock polling loop
Test runtime for that test drops from a up-to-5s poll to near-instant

corrections: StreakStateProvider.watch() drives the wait via a Drift .watch() stream plus async restoreIfEmpty, independent of clock source. Injecting a fixed clock fixes the DateTime.now() seed-anchoring (real, valid benefit) but likely won't make the test 'near-instant' as the acceptance criteria states — some bounded wait for the DB stream's first emission would still be needed. Core rule violation stands; recommendation's stated payoff is optimistic.
